Chapter 3: Triggers—How Everyday Cues Spark Sharing and Remind People to Talk.
So, we’ve talked about why people love to share things. But have you ever wondered when they're actually most likely to do it? That’s where triggers come in.
Triggers are those little cues all around us—things in our environment that nudge us to think about, or talk about, a product, an idea, or even a habit. These cues could be anything: a certain day of the week, a color you see, a sound you hear, or just something you do every day.
Imagine triggers like mental reminders. Kind of like how the smell of fresh bread suddenly makes you crave a trip to your favorite bakery. Or maybe it’s hearing a song about “Friday” and instantly thinking, “Hey, it’s almost the weekend!” That’s why, when a song actually mentions “Friday,” people are way more likely to play it—and share it—at the end of the week. The day itself becomes a trigger, keeping that song stuck in your head and on your playlist.
The wild thing about triggers is how automatic they are. You don’t even have to try—your surroundings do the job for you. That’s why products and ideas that latch onto everyday cues spread so much faster. They basically weave themselves into your daily routine.
So, if you want something to catch on, you need to link it to triggers people bump into all the time. The more often you see or hear a trigger, the more chances you’ll have to remember—and talk about—that product or idea. Think about peanut butter and jelly. Every time someone makes a PB&J sandwich, they’re reminded of their favorite peanut butter brand. That’s a trigger in action.
Triggers can even be tied to seasons or special events. Maybe you’ve noticed how some products get super popular during summer, or how brands jump on the buzz around big sporting events. That’s no accident—it’s all about connecting to moments when people are already paying attention.
But here’s the catch: not all triggers are created equal. The best ones? They’re both frequent and really relevant to whoever you’re trying to reach. A daily cue is way more powerful than something that pops up once in a blue moon. And you need the trigger to be tightly linked to your product or idea, so that connection becomes automatic.
So, how can you actually use triggers? Well, here are a few practical tips:
Try tying your product or idea to a common activity, a certain time of day, or even a familiar place. Link your messages to things people see or do all the time. And don’t forget to reinforce that connection—over and over—so it sticks.
By making your product or idea part of someone’s daily routine, you’re creating these ongoing reminders that keep it top of mind. And that means people are way more likely to talk about it, and share it, even long after they first heard about it.
Triggers and social currency really go hand in hand. Social currency gives people a reason to share, but triggers make sure that sharing happens, again and again. Put them together, and you’ve got a powerful recipe for making anything catch on.
